title: Antibodies, Complement, Infectious Immunity and Hypersensitivity — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Immunology lectures and Hypersensitivity Reactions study guide

questions.stem: How many heavy and light chains form the basic antibody monomer?

options.label: A
options.text: One heavy and two light chains

options.label: B
options.text: Two heavy and one light chain

options.label: C
options.text: Three heavy and one light chain

options.label: D
options.text: Two heavy and two light chains

options.label: E
options.text: Four heavy and no light chains

questions.why: A conventional immunoglobulin monomer has two identical heavy and two identical light chains linked by disulphide bonds.

notes.A: A conventional antibody has a pair of heavy chains, one associated with each light chain.
notes.B: A single light chain leaves one of the conventional antibody's two arms without its paired light chain.
notes.C: A third heavy chain is not part of the standard monomer, which has two matched heavy–light pairs.
notes.E: Each arm of the conventional monomer includes a light chain. Heavy-chain-only antibodies are specialised exceptions.

questions.stem: Which antibody region largely determines antigen-binding specificity?

options.label: A
options.text: Constant domains of both heavy chains

options.label: B
options.text: Variable regions in both chain types

options.label: C
options.text: Carbohydrate coating of the Fc region

options.label: D
options.text: Terminal region of the J chain

questions.why: Antigen specificity comes mainly from the variable domain of each heavy chain paired with a light-chain variable domain. Their loops together form the antigen-binding surface.

notes.A: Heavy-chain constant domains help determine antibody class and effector function rather than the main binding specificity.
notes.C: Fc glycans can affect effector interactions but do not form the usual antigen-combining site.
notes.D: The J chain helps assemble polymeric IgA and IgM rather than determining antibody specificity.
notes.E: Hinge disulphides maintain antibody architecture but do not provide the binding surface for the antigen.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is usually most abundant in adult serum?
questions.why: IgG accounts for the largest share of immunoglobulin in healthy adult serum. Its concentration in blood is generally higher than that of any other immunoglobulin class.

notes.A: IgM is usually prominent early in a primary response, but its total serum concentration is below IgG.
notes.B: IgA predominates at many mucosal surfaces. Circulating levels are generally lower than IgG.
notes.C: IgE binds mast-cell and basophil receptors with high affinity but is normally scarce in serum.
notes.D: IgD serves as a receptor on naive B cells and is found at low levels in serum.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin normally crosses the placenta to provide passive fetal immunity?
questions.why: Placental neonatal Fc receptor binds and transports maternal IgG across the placental barrier. This gives the fetus temporary antigen-specific protection without requiring its own antibody response.

notes.A: IgM generally remains on the maternal side. Fetal or neonatal IgM can reflect endogenous antibody production.
notes.B: IgA provides mucosal protection, including through breast milk, rather than being the usual transplacental class.
notes.D: IgE is bound by high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils but is not routinely transferred by placental FcRn.
notes.E: IgD is mainly associated with B-cell antigen recognition rather than placental transfer.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is a useful marker of a recent primary immune response?
questions.why: IgM often appears before substantial class-switched antibody in a primary response. A pathogen-specific IgM result can therefore suggest recent infection, although timing and test limitations matter.

notes.B: IgG can appear later in the primary response or persist from prior exposure, so detection alone does not ordinarily establish recent infection.
notes.C: IgA is important in mucosal immunity and is not the general early marker of a primary systemic antibody response.
notes.D: IgE is associated with certain allergic and antiparasite responses rather than a general marker of recent infection.
notes.E: IgD mostly functions as a B-cell surface receptor and is not routinely used to date primary immune responses.

questions.stem: Which antibody is characteristically present as a J-chain-linked pentamer in plasma?
questions.why: Secreted IgM commonly forms a pentamer containing a joining chain. The multiple antigen-binding sites provide high overall avidity for targets displaying repeated epitopes.

notes.A: IgG circulates primarily as a monomer of two heavy and two light chains.
notes.B: Serum IgA is mainly monomeric, whereas secretory IgA is usually a J-chain-linked dimer.
notes.C: IgE ordinarily has a monomeric structure even when held by receptors on mast cells.
notes.E: IgD occurs mainly as a monomeric antigen receptor on naive B cells.

questions.stem: Which antibody class is typically dimeric in mucosal secretions?
questions.why: In mucosal secretions, IgA is usually a J-chain-containing dimer. Transport across epithelium adds a secretory component that helps protect it from degradation.

notes.A: Serum IgG is usually monomeric and does not have the characteristic secretory IgA structure.
notes.C: Circulating IgE is monomeric and is best known for high-affinity binding to mast-cell receptors.
notes.D: Surface IgD is an antigen receptor on naive B cells, rather than the typical mucosal dimer.
notes.E: Monomeric IgM occurs on B cells. Polymeric IgM can be secreted, but it is not the characteristic mucosal IgA dimer.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin has high-affinity binding to mast-cell Fc receptors in immediate allergy?
questions.why: IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells and basophils, enabling rapid allergen-triggered degranulation.

notes.A: IgD is mainly a B-cell antigen receptor and does not bind the high-affinity IgE receptor.
notes.B: IgG binds Fc gamma receptors and can have other effector functions, while classic immediate allergy uses Fc epsilon RI.
notes.C: IgM can activate classical complement efficiently but is not the high-affinity mast-cell antibody in immediate allergy.
notes.D: IgA supports mucosal defence and binds other receptors rather than the mast-cell Fc epsilon receptor.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is commonly expressed with IgM on naive mature B-cell surfaces?
questions.why: Naive mature B cells usually display both IgM and IgD with the same antigen specificity. Alternative RNA processing allows the same rearranged variable region to be expressed with either constant region.

notes.A: IgA is generally expressed after class switching and is prominent in mucosal secretions.
notes.B: IgE is a class-switched antibody associated with immediate allergy and type 2 immune responses.
notes.D: IgG typically appears on B cells after class switching rather than as the standard co-receptor isotype on naive cells.
notes.E: Secretory IgA is transported across epithelium and is not a common antigen receptor on naive B cells.

questions.stem: Which antibody fragment retains the principal antigen-binding sites after proteolytic cleavage?
questions.why: A Fab fragment contains a complete light chain paired with part of the heavy chain. Their variable regions retain a site capable of binding antigen.

notes.B: The Fc fragment contains heavy-chain constant domains that interact with effector molecules and receptors.
notes.C: The J chain participates in assembly of certain polymeric antibodies and does not contribute an antigen-binding site.
notes.D: Secretory component derives from the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor and protects secreted antibody.
notes.E: C3 is a complement protein. Its fragments are distinct from antibody fragments such as Fab.

questions.stem: Why does IgM often strongly activate complement during a primary immune response?

options.label: A
options.text: Its Fc region directly cleaves C3

options.label: C
options.text: It activates only the lectin route

options.label: E
options.text: Its J chain acts as a membrane pore

questions.why: Binding to antigen rearranges pentameric IgM so that several Fc regions can engage C1q efficiently. This initiates the classical complement pathway even early in a primary response.

notes.A: IgM binds the C1 complex but does not itself cleave C3. A downstream convertase performs that reaction.
notes.B: Factor D is a separate protease in the alternative pathway, not a constituent of IgM.
notes.C: Antigen-bound IgM primarily initiates the classical pathway, whereas lectin activation begins with carbohydrate recognition.
notes.E: The J chain helps assemble IgM, whereas the membrane attack pore is formed by terminal complement proteins.

questions.stem: How does a monoclonal antibody preparation differ from a conventional polyclonal antiserum?

options.label: A
options.text: It contains all antibody clones from serum

options.label: B
options.text: It recognizes one defined epitope specificity

options.label: C
options.text: It recognizes many epitopes on one protein

options.label: D
options.text: It cannot recognize any protein antigen

options.label: E
options.text: It lacks an immunoglobulin Fc region

questions.why: A conventional monoclonal preparation comes from one selected antibody sequence. Its molecules share a defined antigen-binding specificity, whereas ordinary antiserum contains products of many B-cell clones.

notes.A: A preparation containing antibodies from all serum clones would be polyclonal.
notes.C: Recognition of many separate epitopes on one protein is typical of antiserum containing several clones.
notes.D: A monoclonal antibody can recognise a protein if its binding site matches an accessible epitope.
notes.E: A conventional whole monoclonal antibody has an Fc region whose structure depends on its isotype.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of fusing an antibody-producing B cell with a myeloma cell?
questions.why: The B cell supplies specificity for the chosen antigen and the myeloma fusion partner supplies sustained proliferation. A selected hybridoma clone can continue secreting the same antibody.

notes.A: Neutrophils are myeloid granulocytes and do not result from fusion of the specified cells.
notes.B: Secretion of the selected antibody is the purpose of producing an antibody-secreting hybridoma.
notes.C: The original B-cell antigen-binding specificity is retained in a selected antibody-secreting clone.
notes.D: A macrophage is from a separate lineage and does not arise from the antibody-producing cell fusion.

questions.stem: Why are unfused myeloma cells unable to persist in aminopterin-containing HAT medium when salvage-deficient?

options.label: C
options.text: They cannot salvage nucleotides under HAT

options.label: E
options.text: They cannot synthesize any nuclear proteins

questions.why: Aminopterin blocks folate-dependent de novo nucleotide synthesis. An unfused myeloma cell deficient in the necessary salvage enzyme cannot make sufficient nucleotides to proliferate in HAT medium.

notes.A: Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP, but the selection depends on nucleotide production for cell growth.
notes.B: IgG degradation is unrelated to the ability to use nucleotide salvage substrates in this selection.
notes.D: CD4 is an immune co-receptor, whereas the growth difference depends on the ability to salvage nucleotides.
notes.E: HAT limits nucleotide synthesis in susceptible cells rather than universally stopping synthesis of nuclear proteins.

questions.stem: Which HAT medium component directly blocks de novo nucleotide synthesis?
questions.why: Aminopterin inhibits folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis, making salvage-dependent selection possible.

notes.B: Hypoxanthine is a purine precursor supplied for nucleotide salvage. It does not block de novo synthesis.
notes.C: Thymidine supplies a precursor for dTMP synthesis through salvage rather than acting as the inhibitor.
notes.D: Biotin is a cofactor in carboxylase reactions and is not the antifolate used in HAT.
notes.E: Glycine contributes atoms to purines during de novo synthesis rather than blocking the pathway.

questions.stem: Which monoclonal antibody design contains murine variable regions joined to human constant regions?
questions.why: A classical chimeric antibody combines the complete mouse-derived variable domains with human constant domains. This retains the original binding site and replaces the constant region with a human one.

notes.A: A fully murine antibody has mouse-derived constant domains as well as mouse-derived variable domains.
notes.B: A humanised antibody has largely human variable frameworks with selected nonhuman binding loops.
notes.C: A fully human antibody has human-derived variable as well as constant regions.
notes.E: Bispecific describes the ability to bind two different targets, independent of the source of the antibody domains.

questions.stem: Which antibody design typically retains mainly murine complementarity-determining regions in a human framework?
questions.why: Humanisation usually retains nonhuman complementarity-determining regions within largely human variable domain frameworks. The retained loops help preserve recognition of the original antigen.

notes.A: A fully murine antibody has mouse-derived frameworks, binding loops and constant regions.
notes.C: A classical chimeric antibody retains complete nonhuman variable domains rather than mainly the binding loops.
notes.D: A fully human antibody uses human-derived sequences for its variable domains, including their binding loops.
notes.E: Polyclonal serum contains immunoglobulins from many clones rather than one defined humanised design.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a conjugated monoclonal antibody from a naked monoclonal antibody?

options.label: E
options.text: An attached drug or radioactive payload

questions.why: A conjugated monoclonal antibody carries an added payload, such as a cytotoxic drug or radionuclide. Antigen recognition can help deliver that payload to selected targets.

notes.A: Antigen binding is generally needed to localise the payload. Conjugation does not remove the binding region.
notes.B: The presence of an attached payload defines conjugation regardless of how the original antibody is produced.
notes.C: Conjugated antibodies can retain heavy chains. Attachment of the payload is the relevant distinction.
notes.D: Binding soluble haptens can occur without conjugation and does not define the type of antibody drug.

questions.stem: What allows a bispecific antibody to bring two different targets into proximity?

options.label: E
options.text: Two covalently attached vitamin K groups

questions.why: A bispecific antibody has binding regions designed for two distinct targets. It can bind both at once and thereby bring the two molecules or cells into proximity.

notes.A: Identical binding domains generally confer one shared specificity rather than two distinct ones.
notes.B: A complement pore disrupts membranes and does not create two antibody binding specificities.
notes.D: A single free heavy-chain fragment does not ordinarily supply two independent antigen-binding sites.
notes.E: Vitamin K groups are unrelated to antigen recognition by an antibody's variable regions.

questions.stem: Which event initiates the classical complement pathway most directly?
questions.why: The classical pathway typically starts when C1q binds appropriately arranged Fc regions of antigen-bound IgM or IgG. This activates associated C1 proteases and begins downstream complement cleavage.

notes.B: Mannose-binding lectin binding to a suitable carbohydrate initiates the lectin pathway.
notes.C: Factor B binds C3b during formation of the alternative-pathway convertase.
notes.D: C5b is generated downstream and recruits terminal complement components to form the membrane attack complex.
notes.E: Properdin can stabilise the alternative convertase, while factor H is primarily a regulator of alternative-pathway activity.

questions.stem: Which complex functions as the classical-pathway C3 convertase?
questions.why: Classical activation cleaves C4 and C2, allowing C4b and the enzymatic C2 fragment to form C4b2a in conventional nomenclature. The complex cleaves C3.

notes.A: C3bBb is the C3 convertase of the alternative pathway rather than the classical pathway.
notes.B: C5b-9 is the terminal membrane attack complex and is formed after C5 cleavage.
notes.C: C1q with C1r and C1s starts classical activation, leading to downstream convertase assembly.
notes.E: C3bBb with another C3b is an alternative-pathway C5 convertase rather than the classical C3 convertase.

questions.stem: Which complex functions as the alternative-pathway C3 convertase?
questions.why: Factor B binds C3b and is cleaved by factor D. The remaining Bb fragment forms the alternative pathway C3 convertase with C3b.

notes.A: C4b2a is the C3 convertase of the classical and lectin pathways rather than the alternative pathway.
notes.C: C5b-9 forms a terminal pore rather than acting as a convertase for C3.
notes.D: C1q, C1r and C1s form the initiating complex of the classical pathway.
notes.E: Adding C3b to C4b2a forms the classical or lectin C5 convertase, not the alternative C3 convertase.

questions.stem: Which plasma enzyme cleaves factor B after it binds C3b in the alternative pathway?
questions.why: Factor D cleaves factor B only after factor B associates with C3b or a related activated C3 form. Retained Bb then acts as the catalytic subunit of the convertase.

notes.A: Factor I is a regulatory protease that inactivates C3b and C4b with suitable cofactors.
notes.B: Factor H regulates the alternative pathway and can help factor I inactivate C3b, rather than cleaving factor B.
notes.C: C1s cleaves C4 and C2 in the classical pathway rather than cleaving C3b-bound factor B.
notes.D: Activated factor XIII cross-links fibrin in coagulation and is not the complement protease asked for.

questions.stem: Which lectin pathway protein recognizes microbial mannose-rich carbohydrates?
questions.why: Mannose-binding lectin recognises characteristic arrangements of carbohydrates on microbial surfaces. Its associated proteases then initiate cleavage events that lead to lectin-pathway C3 convertase assembly.

notes.A: Factor H mainly regulates alternative-pathway complement rather than initiating the lectin pathway on mannose-rich surfaces.
notes.B: IgD is a B-cell antigen receptor isotype rather than a soluble lectin-pathway recognition protein.
notes.D: C-reactive protein is an acute-phase protein that can engage classical complement. It is not the mannose-binding lectin.
notes.E: Thromboxane synthase makes a lipid mediator used in haemostasis rather than recognising carbohydrates for complement activation.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment binds microbial surfaces and enhances their phagocytic uptake?
questions.why: C3 cleavage exposes a reactive group in C3b that can attach to nearby surfaces. Phagocyte complement receptors recognise deposited complement fragments and promote uptake.

notes.B: C3a is a soluble inflammatory fragment rather than the major surface-bound C3 opsonin.
notes.C: C5a is a potent inflammatory mediator and chemoattractant rather than the principal complement coating for phagocytosis.
notes.D: C4a is a small cleavage product and does not provide the major surface-bound opsonin described here.
notes.E: C9 contributes to the terminal pore and is not the main tag that promotes phagocytic uptake.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment is a potent chemoattractant and inflammatory mediator?
questions.why: C5 convertases release soluble C5a, a strong anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant. It activates leukocytes and guides cells such as neutrophils towards sites of complement activation.

notes.A: C3b is mainly associated with surface opsonisation and downstream convertase formation.
notes.B: C4b is deposited on surfaces and participates in the classical and lectin C3 convertase.
notes.C: C5b initiates terminal membrane attack complex assembly rather than acting as the soluble chemoattractant.
notes.E: C9 polymerises in membrane attack pores and does not provide the inflammatory recruitment signal.

questions.stem: Which group of components forms the terminal membrane attack complex?
questions.why: C5b associates with C6 and C7, recruits C8 and enables C9 to assemble into a membrane pore. These terminal components form the membrane attack complex.

notes.A: C1q and associated C1 proteases initiate classical complement rather than forming the terminal pore.
notes.C: C2 and C4 fragments have early roles in convertase formation rather than assembling the membrane attack complex.
notes.D: Factors B and D help generate the alternative-pathway convertase.
notes.E: Small cleavage products such as C3a and C5a act as soluble mediators rather than pore subunits.

questions.stem: Which complement pathway can be initiated on microbial surfaces without antigen-specific antibody?
questions.why: Alternative-pathway tick-over and surface amplification can operate independently of antibodies.

questions.stem: What is the principal difference between classical and lectin complement activation at the initiating step?

options.label: D
options.text: MHC class I versus MHC class II

questions.why: Classical activation commonly starts with C1q recognising clustered Fc regions on antibody-coated targets. Lectin activation instead starts with lectins or ficolins recognising characteristic surface carbohydrates.

notes.A: Thrombin and plasmin act in coagulation and fibrinolysis rather than defining these two complement initiation mechanisms.
notes.B: Immediate IgE signalling involves mast-cell receptors, whereas the complement routes here differ in how they recognise the activating surface.
notes.D: MHC molecules are used to display antigens to T cells, rather than to initiate these complement pathways.
notes.E: Lymphocyte maturation generates immune cell populations, while the distinction here concerns soluble recognition proteins.

questions.stem: Why may serum complement C3 and C4 concentrations fall during active immune-complex disease?

options.label: B
options.text: The immune complexes permanently synthesize C3

options.label: C
options.text: C3b directly prevents hepatic albumin production

options.label: E
options.text: Immune complexes inhibit hepatic factor synthesis

questions.why: Immune complexes can repeatedly engage the classical complement pathway and promote cleavage of C4 and C3. When consumption outpaces synthesis, their measured serum concentrations can decrease.

notes.B: Immune complexes are assemblies of antigens and antibodies and do not synthesise complement proteins.
notes.C: Reduced complement concentrations in this setting reflect activation and consumption rather than an effect of C3b on albumin production.
notes.D: Mature erythrocytes do not make the circulating complement pool, although they carry some complement-regulating proteins.
notes.E: Complement can decrease despite continued hepatic production, because activation removes intact C3 and C4 from serum.

questions.stem: Which laboratory assay evaluates activity of the classical complement pathway as a functional unit?
questions.why: CH50 measures the ability of serum complement to lyse antibody-sensitised red cells. The assay depends on functional classical and terminal components, so deficiency or consumption can reduce activity.

notes.A: The direct Coombs test detects immunoglobulin or complement coating the patient's own red cells.
notes.B: Prothrombin time measures clotting through parts of the coagulation cascade rather than the function of serum complement.
notes.C: Amylase assays measure activity of a carbohydrate-digesting enzyme and do not test red-cell lysis by complement.
notes.E: A reticulocyte count estimates marrow red-cell output rather than the capacity of complement to lyse indicator cells.

questions.stem: Which innate cytokines help establish an antiviral state in nearby uninfected cells?
questions.why: Type I interferons, especially interferon-alpha and interferon-beta, signal to nearby cells. They induce expression of proteins that help restrict viral replication in those cells.

notes.A: IL-4 promotes type 2 responses and is not the principal inducer of the early interferon-mediated antiviral state.
notes.C: IL-5 promotes eosinophil development and survival rather than inducing the typical antiviral state.
notes.D: Transforming growth factor beta has regulatory effects on inflammation and differentiation rather than defining the type I interferon response.
notes.E: Vascular endothelial growth factor primarily supports angiogenesis and vascular responses.

questions.stem: Which lymphocytes can rapidly attack virus-infected cells before a fully specific T-cell response develops?
questions.why: Natural killer cells can respond to activating signals on infected or stressed cells without prior expansion of an antigen-specific T-cell clone. They release granules that can induce target-cell death.

notes.A: Naive B cells require activation and differentiation before providing substantial newly induced antibody.
notes.B: Long-lived plasma cells secrete antibodies but do not directly kill infected host cells using cytotoxic granules.
notes.C: Basophils are granulocytes associated with immediate allergy and type 2 responses rather than early antiviral cytotoxicity.
notes.D: Regulatory T cells restrain immune responses and are not the principal early innate cytotoxic lymphocytes.

questions.stem: Which adaptive mechanism most directly destroys host cells containing replicating viruses?
questions.why: Infected cells present peptides from intracellular proteins on MHC class I. Virus-specific CD8 T cells recognise the peptide–MHC complex and can trigger the infected cell to die.

notes.A: Secretory IgA can neutralise material at mucosal surfaces but does not directly kill cells harbouring replicating virus.
notes.B: Complement can act on extracellular targets rather than providing antigen-specific killing of infected cells.
notes.D: Neutrophil trapping can aid extracellular bacterial defence and does not explain this adaptive cytotoxic response.
notes.E: IgE-linked eosinophil activity is associated with defence against some helminths and is not the usual antiviral killing pathway.

questions.stem: Which immune mechanism primarily prevents extracellular viruses from attaching to target cells?
questions.why: Neutralising antibodies bind exposed structures on extracellular viral particles. Binding can obstruct attachment to host receptors or another step needed for entry.

notes.B: Inflammasomes are intracellular signalling complexes and do not directly coat viruses before attachment.
notes.C: Mast-cell mediators alter inflammatory responses, but are not the primary means of blocking viral attachment sites.
notes.D: Platelet thromboxane promotes aggregation and vascular responses rather than neutralising extracellular virus.
notes.E: Bradykinin increases vascular permeability and does not specifically block viral binding to receptors.

questions.stem: Which response is particularly effective against encapsulated extracellular bacteria?

options.label: A
options.text: CD8 killing of uninfected epithelial cells

questions.why: A capsule can hinder direct uptake by phagocytes. Antibody and deposited complement fragments mark the bacterial surface for recognition by neutrophils and macrophages.

notes.A: CD8 cells recognise peptides displayed on host cells and are not the main way to clear free encapsulated bacteria.
notes.B: Basophil activation by IgE is part of immediate allergic and type 2 responses, rather than the key opsonic mechanism here.
notes.C: Photopigment bleaching is a response to light in the retina, unrelated to bacterial uptake by phagocytes.
notes.E: Vitamin K supports modification of clotting proteins, but that process does not mark a capsule for phagocytosis.

questions.stem: Which adaptive pathway is especially important against bacteria surviving within macrophages?

options.label: C
options.text: IgE stimulation of mast cells only

questions.why: Th1 cells supply interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages and enhances killing of ingested microbes. This is particularly important for bacteria that can survive inside phagocytes.

notes.A: IL-4 is associated with a type 2 activation programme rather than the interferon-gamma-dependent antimicrobial response.
notes.C: IgE-mediated mast-cell responses act primarily in allergy and some parasite responses, rather than activating infected macrophages.
notes.D: The complement membrane attack complex usually acts on accessible extracellular surfaces and is not the main intramacrophage killing mechanism.
notes.E: Secretory IgA acts at mucosal surfaces and does not substitute for Th1-driven macrophage activation.

questions.stem: A mycobacterium prevents phagosome–lysosome fusion. What defence is thereby evaded?

options.label: B
options.text: Direct lysis by red blood cells

questions.why: Phagosome–lysosome fusion exposes an engulfed microbe to an acidic, enzyme-rich compartment. If fusion is impaired, the phagocyte loses part of its normal intracellular degradative capacity.

notes.A: Antibodies can neutralise extracellular toxins but that process is distinct from degradation after phagocytosis.
notes.B: Erythrocytes mainly carry oxygen and do not perform this lysosomal killing function.
notes.C: Cilia clear particles at the airway surface, before the intracellular phase described in the stem.
notes.D: Retinal chromophore formation is part of the visual cycle and has no role in phagolysosomal killing.

questions.stem: Which response is most strongly associated with defence against helminths?

options.label: A
options.text: Th1, IgG and cytotoxic CD8 cells

options.label: B
options.text: Type I interferons and NK cells

questions.why: Helminths commonly elicit type 2 immunity, involving Th2 cytokines, IgE and eosinophils. This response can aid expulsion and direct inflammatory activity at large parasites.

notes.A: Th1 and CD8 responses are more closely associated with defence against intracellular microbes.
notes.B: Type I interferons and NK cells are prominent in early antiviral responses.
notes.D: Loss of C3 convertase activity impairs complement and does not define a protective antihelminth response.
notes.E: Neutrophil oxidants help kill certain bacteria and fungi, but type 2 immunity is more characteristic of helminth defence.

questions.stem: Which immune cells are prominent in acute defence against many invasive fungal infections?
questions.why: Neutrophils and macrophages recognise and respond rapidly to invading fungi. Neutrophils are particularly important in defence against many invasive moulds, which helps explain the risk associated with neutropenia.

notes.B: Erythrocytes transport oxygen and platelets support haemostasis. Neither is a principal antifungal phagocyte.
notes.C: B cells can contribute antibodies, but acute antifungal defence also depends strongly on innate phagocytes.
notes.D: Photoreceptors detect light and have no general role in controlling invasive fungi.
notes.E: Adrenal cortical cells produce steroids rather than serving as rapid antifungal effector cells.

questions.stem: Why does antigenic variation favour viral persistence or reinfection?

options.label: B
options.text: It reduces antiviral interferon receptor density

options.label: C
options.text: It prevents all replication of viral genomes

options.label: D
options.text: It reduces recognition by existing immunity

questions.why: Existing immune responses recognise particular antigenic features. Naturally occurring antigenic variation can make previous immunity less effective against a variant, contributing to reinfection in some cases.

notes.A: Antigenic variation can change the targets of recognition without changing a virus into a different type of organism.
notes.B: Interferon receptor density is a feature of the host cell and is not the defining effect of antigenic variation.
notes.C: Evasion of some existing responses can favour viral persistence. It does not require loss of genome replication.
notes.E: Variation can affect immune recognition while the host's complement proteins continue to function.

questions.stem: Which immunological mechanism defines type I immediate hypersensitivity?
questions.why: Immediate type I hypersensitivity follows allergen engagement of IgE bound to high-affinity receptors on mast cells or basophils. This can rapidly release histamine and other mediators.

notes.A: Antibody binding to a fixed cell target is characteristic of type II hypersensitivity.
notes.C: Deposition of soluble immune complexes is the classic initiating mechanism in type III hypersensitivity.
notes.D: Sensitised T-cell cytokine release is characteristic of the delayed, type IV category.
notes.E: Complement deficiency can predispose to other disorders, but does not define immediate IgE-mediated hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: Why may a first allergen encounter produce no immediate symptoms but later exposure causes hives?

options.label: A
options.text: First exposure consumes circulating mast cells

options.label: B
options.text: Allergen must first mutate within plasma

options.label: C
options.text: Allergens require a complement C9 pore

questions.why: Initial exposure can induce allergen-specific IgE, which loads high-affinity receptors on mast cells. On re-exposure, the allergen can cross-link this IgE and rapidly trigger hives.

notes.A: Sensitised mast cells remain present in tissues and are required for the rapid response on re-exposure.
notes.B: An allergen does not need to mutate. Prior exposure changes the host's antibody response.
notes.C: C9 forms part of the complement membrane attack complex, whereas hives here arise through mast-cell mediators.
notes.D: Erythrocytes transport oxygen and do not acquire antigen-specific immune memory.

questions.stem: Which event directly triggers degranulation of sensitized mast cells during re-exposure?

options.label: B
options.text: Binding of IgM to erythrocyte antigen

options.label: D
options.text: Formation of memory CD8 T cells

questions.why: A multivalent allergen binds adjacent IgE molecules already attached to Fc epsilon RI. This clusters the receptors and triggers intracellular signals for degranulation.

notes.A: The initiating interaction occurs at the cell surface rather than through formation of intracellular immune complexes.
notes.B: IgM binding to red-cell antigens can activate complement, which is distinct from the immediate mast-cell trigger.
notes.D: CD8 memory can support later cytotoxic responses, but does not trigger mast-cell degranulation.
notes.E: C3 deficiency impairs complement and is not the direct signal for IgE-mediated mast-cell activation.

questions.stem: Which mediator is preformed in mast-cell granules and rapidly causes vascular permeability?
questions.why: Mast cells store histamine in granules and can release it within moments of activation. Histamine acts on local vessels to increase permeability and promote swelling.

notes.B: Leukotriene C4 is a lipid mediator made after activation rather than stored as the principal preformed granule mediator.
notes.C: Prostaglandin D2 is synthesised from arachidonic acid after activation and is not the preformed mediator requested.
notes.D: Platelet-activating factor is a lipid mediator produced on activation rather than the classic preformed granule amine.
notes.E: IL-12 helps direct Th1 responses and is not the granule mediator responsible for this rapid vascular effect.

questions.stem: Which treatment is first-line for life-threatening systemic anaphylaxis?
questions.why: Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Its adrenergic effects counter severe vasodilation and support bronchodilation, addressing cardiovascular and airway compromise.

notes.A: Oral antihistamines can help relieve some skin symptoms, but cannot replace adrenaline for airway or cardiovascular compromise.
notes.B: Corticosteroids act too slowly to reverse the immediate life-threatening features and are not a substitute for adrenaline.
notes.C: Leukotriene antagonists have roles in conditions such as asthma, rather than providing emergency first-line reversal of anaphylaxis.
notes.E: A topical mast-cell stabiliser acts locally and does not rapidly treat systemic shock or airway obstruction.

questions.stem: Which test produces a wheal-and-flare reaction within minutes in a sensitized person?
questions.why: In a sensitised person, allergen at the prick site cross-links IgE on cutaneous mast cells. Rapid histamine release produces the raised wheal and surrounding flare.

notes.A: Tuberculin testing measures delayed T-cell hypersensitivity and is read much later than an immediate wheal-and-flare response.
notes.C: Direct antiglobulin testing detects immunoglobulin or complement already bound to red cells.
notes.D: CH50 is an assay of functional classical complement activity, rather than an immediate cutaneous response to an allergen.
notes.E: The indirect Coombs procedure detects red-cell-reactive antibodies in serum and does not assess cutaneous mast-cell activation.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is characteristic of type II hypersensitivity?

options.label: B
options.text: CD4 T cells respond after two days

options.label: E
options.text: Antibody binds a fixed cell-surface target

questions.why: In type II hypersensitivity, IgG or IgM recognises antigen fixed to a cell surface or extracellular matrix. The response can damage the target or alter receptor function.

notes.A: Soluble immune-complex deposition is characteristic of type III hypersensitivity.
notes.B: A delayed reaction mediated by sensitised T cells belongs to type IV hypersensitivity.
notes.C: IgE cross-linking triggers immediate mast-cell activation and is the mechanism of type I reactions.
notes.D: Secretory IgA neutralisation is a protective mucosal function rather than antibody-mediated injury to a fixed target.

questions.stem: Why can Graves disease be classified as receptor-mediated type II hypersensitivity?

options.label: D
options.text: CD8 cells remove all thyroid follicles

questions.why: In Graves disease, stimulating autoantibodies bind the TSH receptor and mimic part of the normal TSH signal. Antibody action on a fixed receptor makes this a functional type II reaction.

notes.A: Glomerular deposition of circulating immune complexes illustrates a different mechanism, type III hypersensitivity.
notes.B: IgE-dependent mast-cell activation is an immediate type I reaction and does not drive TSH receptor signalling.
notes.D: Destruction of follicles would reduce hormone production, whereas the characteristic autoantibodies increase receptor signalling.
notes.E: Graves hyperthyroidism is linked to receptor stimulation by antibody rather than failure of complement.

questions.stem: Which disease illustrates receptor-blocking rather than receptor-stimulating type II hypersensitivity?
questions.why: In common forms of myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies impair signalling at the neuromuscular junction. Antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor can block, remove or damage receptors, weakening muscle activation.

notes.B: Graves disease is mediated by autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor rather than impairing acetylcholine receptor function.
notes.C: Serum sickness is a systemic immune-complex reaction in the type III category.
notes.D: Allergic contact dermatitis is caused predominantly by antigen-specific T cells in a type IV response.
notes.E: Allergic rhinitis is commonly an IgE-associated type I reaction.

questions.stem: Which laboratory test detects immunoglobulin already bound to erythrocytes in vivo?
questions.why: The direct antiglobulin test uses the patient's red cells. Antiglobulin reagent detects antibody or complement that had already coated those erythrocytes in the circulation.

notes.A: The indirect antiglobulin test assesses serum antibodies capable of binding reagent red cells in vitro.
notes.B: Skin-prick testing detects immediate cutaneous reactivity in a sensitised person.
notes.C: CH50 measures the ability of serum complement to support lysis rather than directly assessing coating of patient cells.
notes.E: Serum IgE measurement quantifies soluble immunoglobulin and does not test for antibody already attached to red cells.

questions.stem: Which immunological event initiates type III hypersensitivity injury?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct IgG binding to a cell receptor

options.label: C
options.text: Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells

options.label: D
options.text: CD8 T-cell recognition of host peptides

questions.why: Soluble antigen–antibody complexes can accumulate in tissues, where they activate complement and recruit inflammatory cells. That local inflammation produces the injury of type III hypersensitivity.

notes.A: Antibody binding directly to a fixed receptor is a type II mechanism.
notes.C: IgE cross-linking on mast cells is the initiating mechanism in type I hypersensitivity.
notes.D: CD8 recognition of peptide on MHC class I can cause T-cell-mediated injury rather than immune-complex deposition.
notes.E: Loss of C9 can impair the terminal complement pore but does not initiate the deposition of immune complexes.

questions.stem: A patient develops fever, arthralgia and rash several days after exposure to foreign serum proteins. What mechanism is likely?
questions.why: In serum sickness, antibodies form against the foreign proteins. The resulting circulating complexes deposit and activate inflammation, explaining the delayed fever, rash and joint symptoms.

notes.A: Immediate mast-cell degranulation usually gives symptoms soon after re-exposure rather than the delayed systemic syndrome described.
notes.B: Binding of antibody to fixed red-cell targets can cause haemolysis, which is a different mechanism.
notes.C: Cytotoxic T cells kill recognised target cells. The combination described is typical of systemic immune-complex inflammation.
notes.D: An inherited complement deficiency may predispose to some conditions but is not required for serum sickness.

questions.stem: What is an Arthus reaction?
questions.why: An Arthus reaction occurs when antigen meets pre-existing antibody locally. Deposited complexes can activate complement and recruit neutrophils, producing focal inflammation at the site.

notes.A: Generalised IgE-dependent shock is systemic anaphylaxis rather than a local immune-complex reaction.
notes.B: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed T-cell reaction and does not require local antibody complexes.
notes.D: Autoantibody action at fixed receptors is a type II mechanism, distinct from the local type III reaction.
notes.E: Complement deficiency can predispose to infections, whereas an Arthus reaction involves local inflammation after immune-complex formation.

questions.stem: Which renal immunofluorescence pattern is typical of immune-complex glomerulonephritis?
questions.why: Immune complexes accumulate in discrete glomerular deposits, giving a granular pattern of immunoglobulin and often complement. Antibody that binds an evenly distributed basement-membrane target can instead stain linearly.

notes.B: Smooth linear staining is typical of anti-glomerular-basement-membrane antibody binding rather than discrete complexes.
notes.C: Deposited complexes contain immunoglobulin and can be detected by staining, rather than showing complete absence of tissue proteins.
notes.D: The usual pattern is granular staining for deposited immunoglobulins, often with complement, rather than isolated IgE bands.
notes.E: Perforin is a cytotoxic granule protein and does not account for the typical glomerular deposits.

questions.stem: Which disease is a classical example of type II antibody binding directly to a basement-membrane antigen?
questions.why: In Goodpasture syndrome, autoantibodies bind a fixed type IV collagen antigen in basement membranes. Renal immunofluorescence often shows linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane.

notes.A: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis involves granular immune-complex deposition rather than direct linear anti-basement-membrane binding.
notes.B: Serum sickness is due to systemic immune-complex formation and deposition.
notes.C: Atopic rhinitis usually involves IgE and mast cells rather than antibodies against basement membrane.
notes.E: The tuberculin reaction is a delayed T-cell response and does not depend on anti-basement-membrane antibody.

questions.stem: What is the principal mediator of type IV delayed hypersensitivity?
questions.why: Previously sensitised T cells recognise antigen and can release inflammatory cytokines or kill target cells. The time required to recruit and activate effector cells gives many reactions their delayed onset.

notes.A: Allergen-specific IgE mediates immediate type I reactions through mast cells and basophils.
notes.C: IgM pentamers can activate classical complement and are not the principal effectors of type IV reactions.
notes.D: Deposited soluble IgG-containing complexes are the trigger in type III hypersensitivity.
notes.E: C3b acts chiefly as a complement-derived surface opsonin rather than the main mediator of delayed hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: When does a typical tuberculin delayed-type skin reaction peak?
questions.why: A tuberculin skin test is generally read 48 to 72 hours after injection. Previously primed T cells recruit inflammatory cells, producing the palpable induration of a delayed reaction.

notes.A: A response within seconds is too early for the characteristic T-cell-dependent induration to develop.
notes.B: A wheal in minutes is typical of immediate allergy testing rather than the delayed tuberculin response.
notes.C: Some early changes can occur within hours, but the usual window for measuring induration is two to three days.
notes.D: Waiting several weeks misses the usual reading window of the local skin reaction.

questions.stem: Which condition best represents a contact dermatitis mediated by type IV hypersensitivity?
questions.why: In nickel allergy, sensitised T cells respond to nickel-associated determinants in skin and induce eczematous inflammation after contact. The mechanism is delayed, type IV hypersensitivity.

notes.A: Immediate food anaphylaxis usually involves activation of IgE-bearing mast cells rather than a delayed T-cell skin response.
notes.B: ABO-incompatible transfusion can cause antibody-mediated destruction of red cells, a type II mechanism.
notes.D: Serum sickness following antitoxin exposure is caused by deposited immune complexes in type III hypersensitivity.
notes.E: Rh haemolytic disease involves maternal antibodies binding fetal or neonatal red cells, a type II reaction.

questions.stem: Which cells most directly mediate tissue injury in a classic Th1-type delayed reaction?
questions.why: In a classic Th1 delayed reaction, antigen recognition induces interferon-gamma and other mediators that recruit and activate macrophages. Activated macrophages then contribute directly to local tissue injury.

notes.B: Erythrocytes carry oxygen and are not the inflammatory effector cells in a Th1 delayed response.
notes.C: Resting platelets participate in haemostasis rather than the macrophage activation that drives this reaction.
notes.D: Neutrophils can contribute to inflammation, but activated macrophages are the characteristic tissue effectors in the classic Th1 pattern.
notes.E: Lens epithelial cells maintain lens function and are not recruited as inflammatory effector cells.
